motion: This House would let kids vote.

claims.claim: Kids deserve a say in decisions that affect their future.
claims.impact: A government answerable to young people invests more in their long-term future.

candidates.text: Politicians chase the votes they need, so youth issues rise up the agenda.
candidates.explanation: Links enfranchising kids to what politicians prioritize.

candidates.text: Places that lowered the voting age saw more youth-focused budget measures.
candidates.explanation: Evidence tying the vote to the investment impact.

candidates.text: A Nobel Prize was awarded for research on voting systems.
candidates.explanation: Authoritative but says nothing about whether kids voting shifts investment.

candidates.text: Kids can already hold part-time jobs in many places.
candidates.explanation: A maturity analogy that doesn't bridge to the investment impact.

impactChoices.text: A government answerable to young people invests more in their long-term future.
impactChoices.explanation: It says what changes in the world, and for a whole generation. That's the so-what.

impactChoices.text: So kids would finally get a say in their future.
impactChoices.explanation: That just repeats the claim. What changes once they have a say?

impactChoices.text: Teens would get real practice using what they learn in civics class.
impactChoices.explanation: A real impact, but it follows from a different claim about civics lessons, not from kids deserving a say.

impactChoices.text: Some kids would feel a bit more included.
impactChoices.explanation: Small and vague. How many kids, and what actually changes for them?

claims.claim: Voting young builds a lifelong habit of participation.
claims.impact: A generation of engaged, lifelong voters strengthens democracy.

candidates.text: Casting a first vote while still in school builds a routine that carries into adulthood.
candidates.explanation: Links early voting to the lifelong-habit impact.

candidates.text: Turnout studies show first voting at 16-17 predicts higher lifelong turnout.
candidates.explanation: Direct evidence for the impact.

candidates.text: Social media use among teens is at an all-time high.
candidates.explanation: A striking stat that doesn't connect to voting habits.

candidates.text: Adults sometimes forget to register.
candidates.explanation: About adults, not about kids building a habit.

claims.claim: Teens learn civics in school right when they could use it.
claims.impact: Voting reinforces classroom civics with real practice, producing better-informed citizens.

candidates.text: Applying civics lessons to a real ballot cements the learning.
candidates.explanation: Links school civics + voting to informed citizens.

candidates.text: Schools with mock-then-real voting programs report higher civic knowledge scores.
candidates.explanation: Evidence for the informed-citizen impact.

candidates.text: Most teenagers own a smartphone.
candidates.explanation: True and modern-sounding, but unrelated to civic knowledge.

candidates.text: Some adults can't name their representatives.
candidates.explanation: A point about adults, not about teens' classroom civics.

claimChoices.text: Kids deserve a say in decisions that affect their future.
claimChoices.explanation: Specific, takes a side, and the other team can fight it. That's a claim.

claimChoices.text: Voting is important.
claimChoices.explanation: A theme, not a stance about kids. The other side has nothing to push against.

claimChoices.text: Kids are affected by laws that adults pass.
claimChoices.explanation: True, but nobody would argue against it. A fact, not a claim.

claimChoices.text: Kids are too young to understand politics.
claimChoices.explanation: That's the AGAINST case. Your claim has to argue for your side.

claims.claim: Most young kids don't yet have the experience to weigh complex trade-offs.
claims.impact: Rushed votes from unprepared voters lead to worse collective decisions.

candidates.text: Big policy choices involve trade-offs that take years of context to judge.
candidates.explanation: Links limited experience to weaker decisions.

candidates.text: Studies show reasoning about long-term trade-offs keeps developing through the teen years.
candidates.explanation: Evidence that the capacity is still forming.

candidates.text: A famous economist won a prize for work on voting paradoxes.
candidates.explanation: Authoritative but about voting math, not kids' readiness.

candidates.text: Kids can already use social media.
candidates.explanation: Unrelated to weighing policy trade-offs.

impactChoices.text: Rushed votes from unprepared voters lead to worse collective decisions.
impactChoices.explanation: It names the consequence for everyone, not just the young voters. That's scale.

impactChoices.text: So kids would be voting without enough experience.
impactChoices.explanation: Repeats the claim. It doesn't say what happens next.

impactChoices.text: Kids would be robbed of their childhood by adult duties.
impactChoices.explanation: Belongs to the 'burden' argument, not the experience one.

impactChoices.text: A few votes might be a little less thought-through.
impactChoices.explanation: Too small to matter. Why would a whole election come out worse?

claims.claim: Younger voters are easier to sway with slogans and pressure.
claims.impact: Elections get decided by manipulation rather than reasoning.

candidates.text: Simple, emotional messaging lands harder when someone has less practice spotting spin.
candidates.explanation: Links persuadability to manipulated outcomes.

candidates.text: Media-literacy research finds younger teens are more influenced by viral claims.
candidates.explanation: Evidence for the manipulation risk.

candidates.text: Voter turnout hit record highs in a recent election.
candidates.explanation: Impressive turnout stat, but says nothing about manipulation.

candidates.text: Adults are sometimes swayed by ads too.
candidates.explanation: About adults; doesn't bridge to kids specifically.

claims.claim: Voting is a serious responsibility that shouldn't be forced on children.
claims.impact: Pushing adult duties onto kids robs them of childhood.

candidates.text: Loading civic obligations onto kids crowds out the freedom to just be a kid.
candidates.explanation: Links the duty to lost childhood.

candidates.text: Child-development guidance warns against overloading kids with adult responsibilities.
candidates.explanation: Evidence for the childhood-burden impact.

candidates.text: Some countries have compulsory voting with heavy fines.
candidates.explanation: Real fact about adults' compulsory voting — not about burdening kids.

candidates.text: Kids get pocket money.
candidates.explanation: Irrelevant to the responsibility burden.

claimChoices.text: Most young kids don't yet have the experience to weigh complex trade-offs.
claimChoices.explanation: Specific and contestable: the other side can argue kids are more capable than this.

claimChoices.text: Letting kids vote is a bad idea.
claimChoices.explanation: A verdict, not an argument. Bad why?

claimChoices.text: Voting involves choosing between candidates.
claimChoices.explanation: Everyone agrees. There's nothing to debate.

claimChoices.text: Voting young builds a lifelong habit of participation.
claimChoices.explanation: That's the FOR case. Your claim has to argue against the motion.

keywords.hint: A total ban, or limits? The strength of the wording matters.

claims.claim: Banning homework gives kids time to rest and be with family.
claims.impact: Better-rested kids have stronger wellbeing and family relationships.

candidates.text: Free evenings mean more sleep and family time.
candidates.explanation: Bridges the ban to the wellbeing impact.

candidates.text: Studies link heavy homework loads to student stress and lost sleep.
candidates.explanation: Evidence for the wellbeing impact.

candidates.text: A widely cited study found homework raises standardized-test scores.
candidates.explanation: Impressive, but it argues FOR homework — wrong direction for this impact.

candidates.text: Homework teaches time management.
candidates.explanation: A different impact; doesn't connect to rest/family.

impactChoices.text: Better-rested kids have stronger wellbeing and family relationships.
impactChoices.explanation: It says what the extra time leads to, for kids in general. That's the so-what.

impactChoices.text: So students would have more free time in the evening.
impactChoices.explanation: Just the claim again. What does the free time lead to?

impactChoices.text: Poorer students would no longer be punished for lacking a quiet home.
impactChoices.explanation: Real, but it's the equity argument's impact, not the rest one.

impactChoices.text: Some kids might be slightly less tired on some days.
impactChoices.explanation: Too small and hedged. Why does this matter at scale?

claims.claim: Homework punishes kids who lack a quiet home or help.
claims.impact: Removing homework narrows the gap between rich and poor students.

candidates.text: Kids without a desk or help fall behind on homework they can't do at home.
candidates.explanation: Links homework to the equity gap.

candidates.text: Achievement-gap research ties homework burden to home resources.
candidates.explanation: Evidence for the equity impact.

candidates.text: The best universities assign heavy reading loads.
candidates.explanation: Prestigious-sounding but irrelevant to K-12 equity.

candidates.text: Some kids enjoy homework.
candidates.explanation: Preference, not the equity bridge.

claims.claim: Without homework, class time can be used for real learning.
claims.impact: Learning concentrated in school leads to deeper understanding.

candidates.text: Teachers can guide practice in class instead of sending it home to struggle alone.
candidates.explanation: Links no-homework to in-class depth.

candidates.text: Some no-homework schools report equal or better comprehension.
candidates.explanation: Evidence for the understanding impact.

candidates.text: The school day is six hours long on average.
candidates.explanation: A neutral fact that doesn't bridge to deeper learning.

candidates.text: Homework can be graded for credit.
candidates.explanation: About grading, not about in-class depth.

claimChoices.text: Banning homework gives kids time to rest and be with family.
claimChoices.explanation: Specific, takes a side, and gives the other team something real to push against.

claimChoices.text: Homework is bad for students.
claimChoices.explanation: A feeling, not a claim. Bad how, and for whom?

claimChoices.text: Homework is work students do outside of class.
claimChoices.explanation: A definition. Nobody disagrees, so there's nothing to argue.

claimChoices.text: Practice at home is how skills actually stick.
claimChoices.explanation: That argues AGAINST the ban. Your claim has to argue for it.

claims.claim: Practice at home is how skills actually stick.
claims.impact: Without homework, students master less and fall behind.

candidates.text: Repeating a skill on your own is what moves it into long-term memory.
candidates.explanation: Links home practice to mastery.

candidates.text: Studies link regular spaced practice to stronger retention.
candidates.explanation: Evidence for the mastery impact.

candidates.text: A widely cited study found homework raises standardized-test scores.
candidates.explanation: Strong and on-topic-sounding, but it measures test scores, not the mastery mechanism claimed here.

candidates.text: Some students dislike homework.
candidates.explanation: A preference, not a bridge to mastery.

impactChoices.text: Without homework, students master less and fall behind.
impactChoices.explanation: It names what happens to students' learning over time. That's the consequence.

impactChoices.text: So students would get less practice at home.
impactChoices.explanation: Restates the claim. What's the consequence of less practice?

impactChoices.text: Students would grow up less organized and disciplined.
impactChoices.explanation: That's the discipline argument's impact, not the practice one.

impactChoices.text: A few students might forget a lesson now and then.
impactChoices.explanation: Trivial. How many students, and what happens over a whole year?

claims.impact: Students grow into organized, independent adults.

candidates.text: Planning and finishing work without a teacher watching builds self-management.
candidates.explanation: Links homework to independence.

candidates.text: Longitudinal studies tie homework routines to later self-regulation.
candidates.explanation: Evidence for the independence impact.

candidates.text: The average backpack weighs several pounds.
candidates.explanation: A concrete-sounding fact with no link to self-discipline.

candidates.text: Homework can be done on a laptop.
candidates.explanation: About tools, not discipline.

claims.claim: Homework lets teachers and parents see where a student is struggling.
claims.impact: Problems get caught and fixed earlier.

candidates.text: Work done alone reveals gaps that in-class group work can hide.
candidates.explanation: Links homework to early detection.

candidates.text: Teachers report using homework patterns to flag students who need help.
candidates.explanation: Evidence for the early-intervention impact.

candidates.text: Report cards are usually issued four times a year.
candidates.explanation: A real fact about grading cadence, not about homework as a signal.

candidates.text: Homework is often graded for points.
candidates.explanation: About grading, not about spotting struggles.

claimChoices.text: Practice at home is how skills actually stick.
claimChoices.explanation: Specific and contestable: the other side can argue practice happens fine in class.

claimChoices.text: Homework is good.
claimChoices.explanation: Good how? There's nothing specific to defend.

claimChoices.text: Teachers assign homework to most students.
claimChoices.explanation: True and undebatable. A fact, not a stance.

claimChoices.text: Homework punishes kids who lack a quiet home or help.
claimChoices.explanation: That's the FOR case. Your claim has to argue against the ban.

motion: This House would require school uniforms.

keywords.hint: Mandatory for everyone, or optional with a default?
A single item like a shirt, or a full standard outfit?

claims.claim: Uniforms hide differences in how much a family can spend on clothes.
claims.impact: Less appearance-based bullying and social division among students.

candidates.text: When everyone dresses alike, expensive brands stop signaling who has money.
candidates.explanation: Bridges uniforms to reduced status signaling and bullying.

candidates.text: Schools that adopted uniforms report fewer clothing-related bullying incidents.
candidates.explanation: Evidence for the bullying-reduction impact.

candidates.text: A famous fashion designer has studied how color affects mood.
candidates.explanation: Sounds authoritative but is about color psychology, not bullying or wealth signaling.

candidates.text: Uniforms are cheaper to buy in bulk for schools.
candidates.explanation: A cost argument, not a bridge to bullying reduction.

impactChoices.text: Less appearance-based bullying and social division among students.
impactChoices.explanation: It says what changes across the whole school. That's the so-what.

impactChoices.text: So nobody would be able to tell who has expensive clothes.
impactChoices.explanation: Repeats the claim. What changes because of that?

impactChoices.text: Students would feel more pride in belonging to their school.
impactChoices.explanation: Real, but it follows from the shared-identity claim, not this one.

impactChoices.text: A couple of students might get teased a little less.
impactChoices.explanation: Too small. Why does this matter across a whole school?

claims.claim: Uniforms remove the daily task of choosing and judging outfits.
claims.impact: More classroom focus on learning instead of appearance.

candidates.text: Without outfit choices to plan or judge, mornings and class time shift toward schoolwork.
candidates.explanation: Links removing outfit decisions to more focus on learning.

candidates.text: Surveys of uniformed schools show students report less time worrying about clothes.
candidates.explanation: Evidence for the focus impact.

candidates.text: A university study found classroom lighting affects test scores.
candidates.explanation: Authoritative-sounding research, but about lighting, not uniforms or focus.

candidates.text: Uniforms make laundry simpler for parents.
candidates.explanation: A convenience argument, not about classroom focus.

claims.claim: Uniforms give students a visible, shared sense of belonging to their school.
claims.impact: Stronger school pride and community identity.

candidates.text: Wearing the same colors and crest visibly ties students to their school's identity.
candidates.explanation: Links shared dress to school pride.

candidates.text: Schools that introduced uniforms report increases in attendance at school-spirit events.
candidates.explanation: Evidence for the school-pride impact.

candidates.text: Professional sports teams generate billions of dollars in jersey sales each year.
candidates.explanation: Sounds relevant to shared dress, but it's about pro sports merchandising, not school identity.

candidates.text: Some students prefer to express individuality through their clothing.
candidates.explanation: An argument against uniforms, not a bridge to the identity impact.

claimChoices.text: Uniforms hide differences in how much a family can spend on clothes.
claimChoices.explanation: Specific, takes a side, and the other team can argue status shows up anyway.

claimChoices.text: Uniforms are good for schools.
claimChoices.explanation: Good how? There's nothing to argue against.

claimChoices.text: Uniforms mean students wear the same clothes.
claimChoices.explanation: A definition, not a stance.

claimChoices.text: Uniforms strip away a student's ability to express who they are.
claimChoices.explanation: That's the AGAINST case.

claims.claim: Uniforms strip away a student's ability to express who they are through clothing.
claims.impact: Students lose a healthy daily outlet for individuality, which hurts their sense of identity and confidence.

candidates.text: Clothing choice is one of the few everyday ways students get to show their personality, and a uniform removes that outlet.
candidates.explanation: Links the uniform requirement to lost self-expression.

candidates.text: Surveys of students at uniform-free schools report higher scores on measures of self-expression and confidence.
candidates.explanation: Evidence for the identity/confidence impact.

candidates.text: A well-known child psychologist's bestselling book explores how teenagers form identity through many different life experiences.
candidates.explanation: Sounds directly relevant to identity, but it's about identity formation broadly, not specifically about clothing or uniforms.

candidates.text: Uniforms are often made from more durable, long-lasting fabric.
candidates.explanation: About durability, not about self-expression.

impactChoices.text: Students lose a healthy daily outlet for individuality, which hurts their sense of identity and confidence.
impactChoices.explanation: It names what students lose and why it matters to who they become. That's the so-what.

impactChoices.text: So students can't choose their own clothes at school.
impactChoices.explanation: Restates the claim. What does losing that choice do?

impactChoices.text: Families would be forced to spend money on clothes they don't need.
impactChoices.explanation: That's the cost argument's impact.

impactChoices.text: Some students might be a bit annoyed in the morning.
impactChoices.explanation: Too small and vague. What's really at stake?

claims.claim: Requiring a specific uniform forces every family to buy extra, dedicated clothing regardless of what they already own.
claims.impact: Removing the uniform requirement saves low-income families money and reduces financial strain.

candidates.text: When a special outfit is mandatory, families can't rely on hand-me-downs or existing clothes, so they must spend more.
candidates.explanation: Links the mandatory uniform to added household cost.

candidates.text: Surveys of parents at uniform schools report higher yearly clothing costs than parents at schools without a uniform policy.
candidates.explanation: Evidence for the financial-strain impact.

candidates.text: Government data show clothing prices overall have risen faster than inflation in recent years.
candidates.explanation: Sounds directly on-topic for cost, but it's about general clothing inflation, not the added cost created specifically by a mandatory uniform.

candidates.text: Kids grow out of any clothing quickly at this age.
candidates.explanation: True of all clothes, not specific to the added burden a mandatory uniform creates.

claims.claim: Uniforms don't stop status competition — it just shifts to shoes, bags, and accessories.
claims.impact: The promised drop in bullying and appearance-based conflict doesn't materialize, so uniforms add cost without the benefit.

candidates.text: When shirts and pants are identical, students wanting to show off status simply shift to the items a uniform doesn't cover, like shoes or backpacks.
candidates.explanation: Links the uniform to displaced, not reduced, status competition.

candidates.text: Several studies comparing uniform and non-uniform schools find no significant difference in reported bullying rates.
candidates.explanation: Evidence that the anti-bullying benefit doesn't hold up.

candidates.text: A landmark study found strict dress codes are linked to improved classroom attendance.
candidates.explanation: Authoritative-sounding, but about attendance, not about whether uniforms reduce bullying or status competition.

candidates.text: Uniforms are usually made from durable, easy-to-clean fabric.
candidates.explanation: About fabric, unrelated to whether uniforms actually reduce status competition.

claimChoices.text: Uniforms strip away a student's ability to express who they are through clothing.
claimChoices.explanation: Specific and contestable: the other side can argue expression happens in other ways.

claimChoices.text: Uniforms are unfair.
claimChoices.explanation: Unfair how, and to whom?

claimChoices.text: Students have different tastes in clothing.
claimChoices.explanation: Obviously true. Nothing to debate.

claimChoices.text: Uniforms give students a visible, shared sense of belonging.
claimChoices.explanation: That's the FOR case.
